title_eng: Structural insights into clinical large language models and their barriers to translational readiness
abstract:
Background: Despite rapid integration into clinical decision-making, clinical large language models (LLMs) face substantial translational barriers 
due to insufficient structural characterization and limited external validation.
Objective: We systematically map the clinical LLM research landscape to identify key structural patterns influencing their readiness for real- 
world clinical deployment.
Methods: We identified 73 clinical LLM studies published between January 2020 and March 2025 using a structured evidence-mapping approach. 
To ensure transparency and reproducibility in study selection, we followed key principles from the PRISMA 2020 framework. Each study was cate-
gorized by clinical task, base architecture, alignment strategy, data type, language, study design, validation methods, and evaluation metrics.
Results: Studies often addressed multiple early stage clinical tasks—question answering (56.2%), knowledge structuring (31.5%), and disease predic-
tion (43.8%)—primarily using text data (52.1%) and English-language resources (80.8%). GPT models favored retrieval-augmented generation (43.8%), 
and LLaMA models consistently adopted multistage pretraining and fine-tuning strategies. Only 6.9% of studies included external validation, and pro-
spective designs were observed in just 4.1% of cases, reflecting significant gaps in translational reliability. Evaluations were predominantly quantitative 
only (79.5%), though qualitative and mixed-method approaches are increasingly recognized for assessing clinical usability and trustworthiness.
Conclusion: Clinical LLM research remains exploratory, marked by limited generalizability across languages, data types, and clinical environ-
ments. To bridge this gap, future studies must prioritize multilingual and multimodal training, prospective study designs with rigorous external 
validation, and hybrid evaluation frameworks combining quantitative performance with qualitative clinical usability metrics.

Abstract
Background: Despite rapid integration into clinical decision-making, clinical large language models (LLMs) face substantial translational barriers 
due to insufficient structural characterization and limited external validation.
Objective: We systematically map the clinical LLM research landscape to identify key structural patterns influencing their readiness for real- 
world clinical deployment.
Methods: We identified 73 clinical LLM studies published between January 2020 and March 2025 using a structured evidence-mapping approach. 
To ensure transparency and reproducibility in study selection, we followed key principles from the PRISMA 2020 framework. Each study was cate-
gorized by clinical task, base architecture, alignment strategy, data type, language, study design, validation methods, and evaluation metrics.

tion (43.8%)—primarily using text data (52.1%) and English-language resources (80.8%). GPT models favored retrieval-augmented generation (43.8%), 
and LLaMA models consistently adopted multistage pretraining and fine-tuning strategies. Only 6.9% of studies included external validation, and pro-
spective designs were observed in just 4.1% of cases, reflecting significant gaps in translational reliability. Evaluations were predominantly quantitative 
only (79.5%), though qualitative and mixed-method approaches are increasingly recognized for assessing clinical usability and trustworthiness.
Conclusion: Clinical LLM research remains exploratory, marked by limited generalizability across languages, data types, and clinical environ-

validation, and hybrid evaluation frameworks combining quantitative performance with qualitative clinical usability metrics.
Key words: clinical artificial intelligence; clinical decision support; foundation models; large language models; model alignment. 
Introduction
Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly 
through deep learning, have accelerated the integration of AI 
technologies into clinical practice, enabling enhanced diagnosis, 
prognosis, and decision support across diverse health-care 
domains.1–4 Among these advances, large language models 
(LLMs) have emerged as a foundational architecture due to their 
capacity to interpret complex, unstructured clinical data—rang-
ing from electronic health records (EHRs) and clinical notes to 
biomedical signals and imaging.5–8 The past 3 years have wit-
nessed a surge in domain-adapted LLMs tailored for clinical 
applications. OpenAI’s GPT-4 derivatives, Meta’s LLaMA- 
based models, and Google’s Med-PaLM series have demon-
strated strong potential in medical reasoning tasks.9–11 For 
instance, Meta’s LLaMA-2-based models outperformed GPT-4 
on 5 out of 8 clinical benchmarks,12 while Google’s Med-PaLM 
2 and Med-Gemini reached up to 91.1% accuracy on the 
MedQA benchmark, approximating expert-level perform-
ance.13,14 These rapid advances demonstrate the increasing rele-
vance of LLMs in supporting clinical decision-making and 
information retrieval. Yet despite these promising results, the 
structural characteristics essential for clinical translation remain 
poorly understood. Specifically, it remains unclear how different 
structural factors—such as alignment strategies, data modalities, 
and study designs—interact to influence the safety and reliability 
of clinical deployment. Most studies emphasize performance 
metrics without systematically addressing model architecture, 
alignment strategies, data modalities, language bias, or valida-
tion rigor. Critically, the lack of prospective designs and external 
validation raises concerns about the safety, reproducibility, and 
generalizability of clinical LLMs in real-world settings. We ana-
lyzed 73 clinical LLM studies published between 2020 and 
2025 using a structured evidence synthesis approach. Each 
study was categorized by clinical task, model type, alignment 
method, data modality, language use, study design, validation 
strategy, and evaluation metrics. This structured mapping offers 
insights into the developmental trajectories and translational 
readiness of clinical LLMs, while identifying structural priorities 
critical for their safe and effective deployment in health care.
Methods
Study selection and eligibility criteria
We conducted a structured literature search to identify clini-
cal LLM studies published between January 2020 and March 
2025. The search was performed using PubMed with

Studies were eligible for inclusion if they met all of the fol-
lowing criteria: (1) development or adaptation of an LLM 
architecture (eg, GPT, LLaMA, or other LLM variants); (2) 
application to clinical data from real-world health-care set-
tings, including unstructured text (eg, clinical notes, medical 
reports), structured data (eg, patient demographics, lab 
results), or multimodal inputs (eg, medical images with 
reports, bio-signals); and (3) implementation for clinically 
relevant tasks such as medical reasoning, classification, text 
generation, or structured information extraction.
Studies were excluded if they met any of the following cri-
teria: (1) application of LLMs was limited to nonclinical 
domains (eg, genomics, drug discovery, agriculture); (2) use 
of general-purpose LLMs without any domain-specific adap-
tation (eg, no medical pretraining or fine-tuning); (3) studies 
focused solely on benchmarking without clinical task applica-
tion; (4) secondary literature such as reviews, commentaries, 
or editorials.
Figure 1 presents the PRISMA flow diagram of the study 
selection process. The initial search identified 3511 articles. 
After title and abstract screening, 108 studies were retained 
for full-text review, from which 73 studies met the inclusion 
criteria and were included in the final analysis. All screening 
steps were independently conducted by 3 reviewers. In cases 
of disagreement, inclusion or exclusion decisions were made 
through group discussion and consensus.
Analytical framework and categorization
We conducted a systematic analysis of the 73 eligible studies 
by extracting key methodological and design attributes from 
each publication. These included the clinical task, model 
type, alignment strategy, data type, language used, study 
design, validation scheme, and evaluation metrics. Each item 
was independently reviewed by 2 domain experts, and any 
discrepancies were resolved through consensus. To ensure 
analytical consistency across heterogeneous studies, we 
applied tailored grouping strategies based on the level of 
interpretive flexibility inherent in each attribute. High- 
flexibility items—such as clinical tasks, base models—were 
grouped inductively by aggregating semantically aligned con-
cepts and identifying shared terminology. In contrast, low- 
flexibility items—such as study design or validation type— 
were categorized using predefined, mutually exclusive labels. 
Clinical tasks were categorized into 5 domains: question 
answering (QA), diagnosis or prediction, knowledge structur-
ing, reporting or summarization, and multimodal inference. 
Model types were classified based on underlying architecture 
(eg, GPT, LLaMA, or others). Alignment strategies were cate-
gorized into 4 primary types—pretraining (PT) only, fine- 
tuning (FT) only, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and 
parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). In addition, we iden-
tified multistage strategies that integrate 2 or more of these 
primary methods, such as sequential pretraining followed by 
task-specific fine-tuning. We categorized cases where 
prompts were used to influence the model’s output, but 
model parameters were not directly changed as “in-context 
learning.”
Data modalities were labeled as text, structured record, 
image, bio-signal, or multimodal combinations. Language 
use was recorded as English, Chinese, multilingual or lan-
guages other than English or Chinese. Study design was 
coded as retrospective or prospective, and validation type as 
internal, external, or both. Evaluation approaches were clas-
sified as quantitative or qualitative. For alignment strategies, 
instruction tuning and supervised FT were grouped under 
“fine-tuning” unless explicitly distinguished by the original 
authors. Multistage alignment was assigned when both pre-
training and domain-specific FT were performed sequentially. 
Parameter-efficient tuning methods (eg, LoRA, adapters) 
were coded separately only when clearly reported. Studies 
incorporating external retrieval mechanisms—either via 
hybrid prompting or knowledge-grounded generation—were 
classified under the RAG category. Although no formal risk- 
of-bias assessment was conducted, inclusion and categoriza-
tion were performed by domain experts through consensus to 
minimize interpretive ambiguity. Detailed descriptions of the 
categorization framework and classification criteria are pro-
vided in Table S1.
